narrative_idea_gen: Told by his perpetually exasperated personal assistant, this is the story of Dalton Mirova — the most powerful superhero alive and, by his assistant's exhausted estimation, the most emotionally incompetent man on Earth — intercut between his catastrophic teenage years (when he accidentally leveled three city blocks trying to look cool at prom) and the present day, where he's supposed to be redirecting a planet-killing asteroid but keeps abandoning the mission mid-flight to call his estranged mother, convinced she's mad at him because she used a period instead of an exclamation point in a text. The assistant narrates with the mounting horror of someone watching a god-tier being spiral over group chat dynamics while extinction-level seismographs spike in the background, and the reader grasps immediately what Dalton cannot: every world-ending crisis he's ever fumbled traces back to his desperate, farcically destructive need for approval — and the only way he saves eight billion people is by surviving the one battle his powers can't help him win, which is sitting alone in the terrifying silence of not being told he's enough. The asteroid is eighteen hours out, Dalton just ghosted NATO to rehearse an apology speech to his college roommate, and his assistant is narrating this all into a voice memo he's titled "Evidence For The Wrongful Death Suit Against God."

narrative_beats:
# Seven Structural Beats for *Evidence For The Wrongful Death Suit Against God*

---

## Beat 1: The Voice Memo and the Asteroid

**What Happens:** The assistant begins recording. He identifies himself, the date, the time remaining until asteroid impact (eighteen hours), and the fact that his boss — the most powerful superhero alive — has just ghosted NATO to rehearse an apology speech to his college roommate. The assistant establishes the dual timeline: he is going to explain how they got here by telling us about Dalton Mirova's prom night, because it is "the same story," and if anyone finds this recording after the extinction event, they should understand that humanity did not die from a cosmic accident but from one man's pathological need to be liked.

**Narrative Technique:** *Frame-as-thesis*, directly modeled on Lispector's opening title-announcement. Where Lispector says "This story could be called 'The Statues,'" the assistant says, in effect, "This is a wrongful death suit against God." The frame precedes and recontextualizes everything that follows. The voice memo format does triple duty: it is (a) a comedic device (the exhaustion, the bureaucratic absurdity of documenting apocalypse), (b) a narrative justification for the assistant's total access to Dalton's inner life and history, and (c) an *unreliable confessional mode* — the assistant claims to be an objective witness but is, from the first sentence, building a case, which means every detail he selects is argumentative. The dual timeline is announced here but not yet activated; the reader is told the past and present are the same story and must hold that claim in suspense.

**Why It Must Work This Way:** The reader needs to know, immediately, that the stakes are simultaneously cosmic (asteroid) and absurdly intimate (a period instead of an exclamation point in a text). The comedy lives in the gap between those two scales, but the structural promise is that the gap will close — that by the end, the reader will understand the text-message crisis and the asteroid crisis are not just parallel but causally linked. The voice memo frame also solves the Lispector problem of who is speaking and why: this is a man who knows he might die in eighteen hours and is compelled to *explain* — not to save himself, but to make someone, anyone, understand the pattern he has been trapped inside. That compulsion to narrate mirrors Lispector's compulsion to retell. The assistant is, without knowing it, performing the same act as Lispector's narrator: circling a single irreducible truth (Dalton's need) and finding that no single angle of approach is sufficient.

---

## Beat 2: The Prom — Defamiliarization of Destruction

**What Happens:** The assistant tells the prom story. Dalton, age seventeen, newly superpowered and not yet in control, attends prom because a girl he likes — or more precisely, a girl whose approval he desperately wants — made a noncommittal comment that he interpreted as an invitation. At the dance, he perceives a slight (she dances with someone else, she doesn't compliment his suit, something equivalently trivial), and in his emotional spiral, his powers discharge. Three city blocks collapse. No one dies — this is crucial, the assistant notes with grim specificity, because Dalton's powers have always been miraculously non-lethal to bystanders, as if the universe itself is enabling him. But three blocks are rubble. And Dalton's first reaction, standing in the dust and ruin, is to ask someone nearby: *"Do you think she's mad at me?"*

**Narrative Technique:** *Defamiliarization through scale inversion.* Where Lispector transforms dead cockroaches into statues (small thing made grand), here the technique is reversed: a city-leveling catastrophe is rendered through the lens of adolescent romantic anxiety (grand thing made small). The assistant narrates the destruction with the flat, dissociated precision of someone who has reviewed this footage too many times — he knows the damage radius, the insurance claims, the FEMA classification — but he also narrates Dalton's emotional state with agonizing empathy despite himself. The comedy is structural: the reader is receiving simultaneously a disaster report and a coming-of-age humiliation story, and they are the same document. The assistant's narration should carry the specific exhaustion of someone who finds the destruction genuinely distressing but who has come to understand that describing the destruction without describing the feelings that caused it would be like describing a flood without mentioning rain.

**Why It Must Work This Way:** This is the baseline instance — the ur-text of the Dalton pattern. Every subsequent beat (past or present) will be a variation on this scene: Dalton perceives an emotional slight, Dalton spirals, Dalton's powers convert interior chaos into exterior catastrophe, Dalton remains focused on the slight. The reader must see the pattern established in its most raw and juvenile form so that when the same pattern recurs in a forty-year-old man with a planet-killer bearing down, the comedy has a backbone of horror. Like Lispector's first telling (the statues), this version of the story is the most aesthetically accessible — it is funny, vivid, almost slapstick. The deeper implications are present but not yet insisted upon. The assistant, at this point, is still narrating *about* Dalton. He has not yet turned the lens on himself or on the reader.

---

## Beat 3: The Asteroid Briefing — Repetition as Reframing

**What Happens:** Cut to present. The assistant describes the NATO briefing forty-eight hours ago, when the asteroid was first confirmed. Dalton was heroic, assured, radiant — the room believed in him, the cameras loved him, the world exhaled. Then, during the briefing, his phone buzzed. His mother's text. The period. "Ok." Not "Ok!" — "Ok." The assistant watched, in real time, as Dalton's focus drained from his face like blood from a wound. Within ninety minutes Dalton had called his mother eleven times (no answer), texted his sister asking "is Mom weird with you too?", and begun composing a seven-paragraph message he would never send. The asteroid continued its approach. Dalton, who can benchpress a tectonic plate, sat on the floor of a Pentagon hallway staring at a phone screen.

**Narrative Technique:** *Repetition with variation — the Lispector master move.* This is the prom again. Every structural element recurs: a high-stakes situation (prom / asteroid), a trivial perceived slight (the girl / the period), a spiral, a disproportionate response. But the register has shifted entirely. The prom was slapstick; this is dread. The assistant narrates with the same factual precision but now the facts are terrifying: eighteen hours, eight billion lives, and the most powerful being on Earth is emotionally flatlined over punctuation. Where Beat 2 invited laughter, Beat 3 withdraws the permission to laugh. The assistant himself signals this shift — his voice memo becomes less sardonic, more strained. He is no longer performing exasperation for comedic effect; he is exasperated because he is frightened. The intercut structure here should create a *palimpsest* effect: the reader sees the Pentagon hallway and the ruined prom superimposed, and the superimposition itself is the argument. *It is the same story.*

**Why It Must Work This Way:** Lispector's genius in Beat 3 ("The Murder") was to retell the same event and reveal that the first telling was a euphemism. The same must happen here. The prom story, told first, felt like a funny origin myth. Retold through the asteroid crisis, it is revealed as a diagnosis. The reader's interpretive frame shifts: this is not a comedy about an overpowered man-child; it is a tragedy (or a tragicomedy) about a person whose interior architecture was never built to bear the weight of the power placed on it. The structural repetition forces the reader to do the diagnostic work themselves — Lispector never explains the connection between her retellings; neither should the assistant. He simply places the two versions side by side and lets the pattern scream.

---

## Beat 4: The Catalogue of Disasters — The Ritual Dimension

**What Happens:** The assistant, with the manic energy of someone who has been holding this in for years, rattles through a compressed litany of Dalton's other catastrophes — all following the same pattern. A bridge collapse in São Paulo (he thought his teammate's birthday toast was sarcastic). A tidal disruption off the coast of Japan (his therapist cancelled a session and he decided this meant he was "too much"). A partial dam failure in Colorado (he read a negative comment about himself online, written by a thirteen-year-old). The assistant delivers these in a kind of incantatory catalogue, each one structured identically: the trigger (always social, always trivial), the spiral, the collateral damage, and Dalton's first words afterward (always about the trigger, never about the damage). The rhythm becomes liturgical. The pattern becomes undeniable.

**Narrative Technique:** *Liturgical catalogue / ritual incantation*, directly paralleling Lispector's Beat 4, where the cockroach killing takes on the quality of ceremony. The repetitive structure of the catalogue — trigger, spiral, damage, oblivious response; trigger, spiral, damage, oblivious response — creates a rhythmic, almost hypnotic effect. The assistant is not telling stories anymore; he is chanting evidence. The voice memo becomes a litany of saints, except the saints are catastrophes and the relics are FEMA reports. The humor darkens with each iteration because the structure itself teaches the reader to anticipate the next disaster, making them complicit in the pattern — we are laughing at a cycle we now recognize we cannot break. The assistant's tone here should achieve the Lispectorian quality of "secret satisfaction": he takes a dark, exhausted pleasure in the completeness of the catalogue, in the elegance of the pattern, and that pleasure disturbs him.

**Why It Must Work This Way:** Lispector's fourth telling revealed the ritual dimension — the fact that the narrator *enjoyed* the killing and that the enjoyment had the structure of ceremony. Here, the ritual being exposed is not Dalton's but the reader's (and the assistant's). We have been *watching this pattern repeat for years and doing nothing.* The catalogue forces the reader to confront what the assistant has already confronted: that Dalton is not failing randomly; he is performing the same sacrifice on an altar of approval, and the entire apparatus of superhero mythology — the costume, the saves, the public adoration — is itself the ritual that enables the cycle. The collateral damage is the offering. The trigger is the call to worship. The pattern is so precise it is theological, which is why the assistant's voice memo is addressed to God.

---

## Beat 5: The Assistant Turns the Lens — Confronting Complicity and the Core Wound

**What Happens:** The timeline collapses. The asteroid is twelve hours out. Dalton has abandoned his flight trajectory for the third time and is now sitting on the roof of a Wendy's in suburban Maryland, calling his estranged mother, who is not picking up. The assistant is in a monitoring van a mile away. And here — this is the story's emotional climax — the assistant stops narrating Dalton's failures and begins narrating his own. He confesses: he has managed the pattern. He has enabled it. Every time Dalton spiraled, the assistant was the one who provided the reassurance that re-stabilized him just enough to finish the mission. *"You're doing great, Dalton."* *"She's not mad, Dalton."* *"Everyone loves you, Dalton."* The assistant is Dalton's emotional insulin pump, and he has kept this man functional without ever once pushing him toward actual healing, because healing would be slow and uncertain and the world always needs saving *right now.* The confession deepens: the assistant also admits, haltingly, that he understands the need. Not Dalton's power — his *need.* The assistant has spent his entire career orbiting a man who craves approval, and he has never once asked himself why he chose that orbit. The voice memo, he realizes aloud, is not evidence against Dalton. It is evidence against himself. He is the one who kept giving the recipe instead of addressing the cockroaches.

**Narrative Technique:** *Collapse of narrative distance*, mirroring Lispector's Beat 5 where the narrator confronts her own joy. The assistant has maintained an ironic, exasperated, observational distance for four beats. Here it disintegrates. The voice memo, which began as sardonic documentation, becomes genuine confession. The sentences should fragment, become recursive, lose their comedic timing. The assistant starts sentences he cannot finish. He contradicts himself. He circles back. The Lispector technique — free indirect discourse collapsing into interior monologue — here becomes a *spoken* version: a man talking into a phone and losing control of his own thesis. This is also where the intercut structure pays its deepest dividend: the assistant is simultaneously describing Dalton on the Wendy's roof and remembering Dalton at prom, and he realizes he has been telling the same story *about himself* all along — the story of a person who manages someone else's emotional catastrophe because managing is easier than feeling.

**Why It Must Work This Way:** Without this beat, the story is a comedy about an incompetent superhero. With it, the story becomes about the ecosystem of emotional avoidance — the fact that Dalton's wound requires enablers, and the enablers have wounds of their own. Lispector's narrator could not stop at admiring the statues; she had to confront her joy in making them. The assistant cannot stop at mocking Dalton; he must confront his participation in the cycle. This beat also sets up the climax: if the assistant has always been the one who provides the reassurance that gets Dalton through the mission, then the only way Dalton saves the world *this time* is if the assistant *doesn't* provide it — if he forces Dalton, and himself, into the silence of not being told they're enough. The stakes of the next beat are now existential for both characters: the assistant must choose to stop enabling, and he must do so knowing that withdrawal might mean Dalton spirals fatally and eight billion people die. The worst-case scenario for the world and the only possible path to healing are the same action.

---

## Beat 6: The Silence — The Battle That Cannot Be Narrated

**What Happens:** The asteroid is six hours out. Dalton has to go *now.* The assistant drives to the Wendy's roof. He finds Dalton mid-spiral — phone in hand, unsent message to his mother glowing on the screen, tears on his face, powers flickering like a brownout. Dalton asks the question he has always asked, in every version of this story, since prom: *"Do you think she's mad at me?"* — or its present equivalent: *"Just tell me it's fine. Just tell me I'm okay."* And the assistant, for the first time in his career, does not answer.
narrative_story:
# Evidence for the Wrongful Death Suit Against God

---

This is a voice memo. I want that stated at the top because I don't know what format this will be in by the time anyone finds it — if anyone finds it — and I want the record to reflect that I'm speaking this aloud, in real time, into a phone with eleven percent battery, in the back of a government-issued Chevy Suburban that smells like someone else's Subway sandwich, at 9:47 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on what may or may not be the last Thursday in the history of Thursdays.

My name is Glen Pasternack. I am — was — am the senior personal aide to Dalton Mirova, known publicly as Paladin, known to the United States Department of Defense as Asset One, known to me as the reason I have been on beta-blockers since I was thirty-one. I have held this position for twelve years. In that time I have managed his calendar, his public statements, his dietary restrictions, and the exposed wiring of his emotional life. I have a GS-14 pay grade and no dental.

The asteroid — I should say this clearly — the asteroid designated 2041 QM7 is approximately eighteen hours from impact. Projected strike zone is the mid-Atlantic, which sounds almost gentle until you learn that "mid-Atlantic impact" is a polite way of saying "the ocean turns into a wall and Europe and the Eastern Seaboard both stop existing, and then the dust blots out the sun, and then everything else stops existing too, more slowly and worse." This has been confirmed independently by NASA, ESA, the Chinese National Space Administration, and a guy at Caltech who, when the numbers came back, reportedly said "Oh" and then sat down on the floor of his lab and didn't get up for forty-five minutes. The point being: this is real.

Dalton can stop it. I want that on the record too. Dalton can fly at speeds that embarrass physics. Dalton can exert force sufficient to redirect a body of that mass if he intercepts it far enough out. Dalton is the only thing on this planet, or off it, that constitutes a viable response. NATO knows this. The Joint Chiefs know this. The Secretary-General gave a televised address four hours ago in which he said, with the grim composure of a man who has been told to project calm while his hands shake below the podium, that "our greatest protector is rising to meet this challenge as we speak."

Our greatest protector is not rising to meet this challenge.

Our greatest protector is currently sitting in a Courtyard by Marriott in Arlington, Virginia, rehearsing — and I need you to absorb this fully — *rehearsing an apology speech to his college roommate, Todd*, because Todd's wife told Dalton at a barbecue in 2038 that Todd had felt "a little abandoned" after Dalton moved to D.C., and Dalton has decided, tonight, eighteen hours before the possible end of all human life, that he cannot leave the planet's atmosphere without first getting this right, without first making sure the phrasing adequately conveys remorse without being "too heavy," because — and this is a direct quote from eleven minutes ago — "If I go up there and I don't come back, I need Todd to know I heard him. I can't die with Todd thinking I didn't hear him."

Todd, for context, could not pick Dalton out of a lineup. I have met Todd. Todd has season tickets to the Nationals and a Traeger grill he won't shut up about and the emotional interior of a golden retriever. Todd is fine. Todd has been fine his entire life. Todd does not lie awake at night wondering whether Dalton Mirova heard him. Todd said "a little abandoned" the way you say "a little chilly" when someone else controls the thermostat — it was an observation, not a wound. But Dalton received it as a wound. Dalton receives everything as a wound.

And now: the world.

I'm going to explain how we got here. I'm going to do it by telling you about Dalton's prom night, because it's the same story. It has always been the same story. If you're listening to this after the impact — if "after the impact" is a thing that exists, if there is anyone left with ears and a device that plays .m4a files — I need you to understand that humanity did not die because of a rock. Rocks are honest. Rocks have trajectories that can be calculated and they do not deviate from those trajectories because their mothers used a period instead of an exclamation point. Humanity, if it dies, will die because a man who could bench-press a tectonic plate never once in his life developed the ability to sit with the possibility that someone, somewhere, might be mildly disappointed in him.

This is my evidence. This is my testimony. If there's a court, if there's anything after this that resembles accountability— God, the universe, whoever signed off on giving *this particular man* the power to move mountains and the emotional stability of a sand castle at high tide — I want this on the record.

Consider it a wrongful death suit.

Against God.

---

Dalton Mirova was seventeen years old. I wasn't there — he was before my time — but I've seen the footage so many times that it's replaced whatever real memories I might've had of my own prom, which is fine, because I didn't go to mine, because I was the kind of person even then who stayed home doing something practical while everyone else did something human, but we'll get to that.

The footage is from three sources: the school's security cameras, a local news helicopter that arrived after, and the dashboard camera of a Berks County sheriff's deputy who was parked across the street eating a hoagie when the event occurred. I've watched all three angles. I've synced them. I could narrate this in my sleep and I have, in fact, narrated it in my sleep, according to two ex-girlfriends and one ex-boyfriend, all of whom left me for reasons that are becoming clearer to me as I sit in this car.

Here is what happened:

Dalton's powers had manifested about four months earlier. He was still new to them. He could fly, but not well — the early footage looks like someone threw a person and the person kept disagreeing with gravity without offering a coherent alternative. He was strong, but the strength was erratic, tied to his adrenaline, emotional in a way that the later military testing would confirm and the DoD would spend a fortune trying to train out of him, unsuccessfully, because you cannot train a river not to flow downhill.

There was a girl named Margaux Kimble. This is a real name — it's been in the public record since the Congressional hearings, so I'm not revealing anything — and I want to be precise about what Margaux Kimble did and did not do, because what she did and did not do is the entire point.

What Margaux Kimble did: She said to Dalton, in the hallway outside AP Chemistry, approximately nine days before prom, "It would be funny if you came." She said this. Multiple witnesses confirm it. She was talking to a small group, not to Dalton specifically, but Dalton was in the group, and she made eye contact with him briefly — briefly — during the word "funny."

What Margaux Kimble did not do: She did not ask Dalton to prom. She did not indicate romantic interest. She did not say "you" to Dalton specifically. She used a conditional. "It would be funny if you came." This is, grammatically and socially, one of the lowest-commitment utterances available in the English language. It is the verbal equivalent of a shrug.

Dalton went to prom.

He wore a suit his mother had helped him pick out — navy, slightly too big in the shoulders, which is heartbreaking in retrospect because his shoulders would later become the thing that stopped a cargo ship from capsizing in the Strait of Malacca, but at seventeen they were just shoulders that hadn't figured out what they were yet. He had a haircut. He had clearly, based on the security footage, applied cologne, because you can see the way he keeps unconsciously turning his own wrist toward his nose as he walks in, checking, rechecking. He walked into that gym the way anyone walks into a room where the person they want is going to be — he walked in like the room was a question and he was hoping to be the answer.

Margaux Kimble was already there. She was with friends. She was wearing a green dress, which I mention only because Dalton mentioned it in his Congressional testimony seven years later, unprompted, in the middle of a question about structural damage estimates, which tells you everything.

What happened next: Nothing. That's what happened. Margaux said hi. Margaux danced with other people, because she had come with other people, because she had not come with Dalton, because she had not asked Dalton, because "it would be funny if you came" is not an invitation. Margaux, at one point, looked at Dalton across the room, smiled in the benign, unfocused way you smile at someone you vaguely recognize, and turned back to her friends.

Dalton stood near the bleachers for approximately forty minutes.

I've watched those forty minutes more than anything else. The security camera in the northwest corner of the gym has the best angle, and if you pull the footage and watch his face — really watch it — you can see something happening that I don't have the vocabulary for, that I'm not sure anyone has the vocabulary for. He isn't angry. He isn't crying. He's *recalculating.* You can see it. Every few seconds his expression shifts, like he's running a new simulation: *Maybe she didn't see me. Maybe I should go over there. Maybe I should wait. Maybe that smile meant something. Maybe it didn't. Maybe I should leave. But if I leave, she'll think I don't care. But if I stay, she'll think I'm desperate. But—* Forty minutes of this. Forty minutes of a seventeen-year-old boy standing next to a folding table of grocery-store cookies, trying to solve an equation that has no solution, because the equation is *Does she like me?* and the answer is *She has not thought about it at all,* and that answer — the null answer, the absence of data — is the one thing his mind cannot metabolize.

What finally triggered the event — and "triggered" is the word used in the DoD file, sanitized, clinical, as if we're talking about a mechanical failure and not a child's heart doing the only thing it knew how to do — was this: Margaux Kimble's date, a boy named Kieran Somebody, put his hand on the small of her back as they walked toward the photo station. That's it. A hand. The small of a back. A universal and essentially meaningless gesture of escort.

Dalton's power discharge was radial. It began at his feet — you can see the gym floor buckle first, the hardwood splitting outward in concentric rings like a stone dropped in a pond — and expanded at a rate that the subsequent physics analysis would clock at roughly two hundred feet per second. The gym walls went first, then the school's east wing, then the street, then the row of shops across from the school — a dry cleaner, a Verizon store, a place that sold custom cakes for occasions exactly like prom. Then the next block. Then the next.

Three city blocks. That's the number. Three blocks of Dalton's hometown reduced to what the insurance industry would later classify, with its particular genius for understatement, as "total structural loss." Forty-seven buildings. Two hundred and twelve vehicles. One small public park with a gazebo where, according to a later lawsuit I helped settle, a couple had been married six hours earlier.

No one died.

I need to sit with this for a moment, because the assistant in me — the functionary, the manager, the man with the clipboard — wants to move past it with a note about miraculous outcomes and move on to the next data point. But the person in me, the version of me that is sitting in this car eighteen hours from possible extinction and has finally run out of professionalism — that person needs to say: nobody has ever died. In twenty-three years and dozens of incidents, across five continents and two oceans and one event that technically occurred in low Earth orbit, no bystander has ever been killed by Dalton's power discharges. Not one. People have been thrown. People have been buried. People have been hospitalized, terrified, displaced. But the casualties column reads zero, and it reads zero every single time, and this is either the most statistically improbable streak in the history of probability or — and this is the part that keeps me up at night, this is the part that makes me address this memo to God, specifically — the power *knows.* It knows where the people are. It goes around them. It flattens buildings and threads the needle around every human body inside, as if the power itself has a conscience that its owner lacks — no, not lacks. Dalton has a conscience. Dalton has too much conscience. That's the whole problem.

It's more like — the power has *priorities* that Dalton doesn't have. The power protects people. Dalton protects himself. And the self he's protecting isn't his body, which is essentially invulnerable, but something much softer and much worse: his idea of himself as someone who is loved.

Three blocks of rubble. Dust still rising. Car alarms singing a twelve-part dissonance.

Dalton, standing in the epicenter, suit torn, looking at the space where Margaux Kimble had been standing (she was fine — she'd been thrown clear, she landed on a pile of gym mats that had been in a storage closet that no longer existed, she had a sprained wrist and a fear of loud noises that would persist for years). And a first responder — a firefighter, the first on scene — approached him and said something. We don't have audio. We have the dashcam, which was across the street at a bad angle. But the firefighter testified later, under oath, about what Dalton said.

The firefighter said: "Son, are you hurt?"

And Dalton said: "Do you think she's mad at me?"

Not: *What happened.* Not: *Is everyone okay.* Not: *Oh God, oh God, what did I do.* Those came later — minutes later, hours later, in the long and genuinely agonized aftermath that I do not want to minimize because Dalton's guilt is real, his guilt is always real, his guilt is the most authentic thing about him. But *first*. Before the guilt, before the horror, before anything else could reach the surface of his consciousness and gasp for air — the question. The only question. The question that has never once, in twenty-three years, not been his first question:

*Am I still loved?*

---

Forty-eight hours ago. The Pentagon. Conference room E-2B-7, which is not its official designation but I don't remember the official designation because my brain has replaced it with the memory of what happened in that room and the designation doesn't matter and nothing matters and I have — okay. Focus.

The briefing was classified COSMIC TOP SECRET, which is a real classification level and which, under the circumstances, was also an unintentional piece of poetry that no one in the room was in a condition to appreciate. Fourteen people. Secretary of Defense. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs. NATO Supreme Allied Commander via secure video. A woman from JPL whose name I didn't catch because she spoke very quietly and I was standing against the wall in my usual position, which is against the wall, which is where the assistant stands, which is where I have always stood.

Dalton was seated at the head of the table. They put him there. They always put him there, and he always does the thing where he says "Oh, I don't need to be at the head" and then sits at the head, and I can never tell if the false modesty is calculated or simply so deeply embedded in his operating system that it *is* his operating system — the constant performance of not wanting what he wants so that someone else will insist he have it.

The JPL woman put up the slides. The asteroid. The trajectory. The mass. The timeline.

I have been in the room for a lot of bad news. I was in the room when the Yellowstone caldera sensors went haywire (false alarm). I was in the room when the Chinese carrier group entered Taiwanese waters (real alarm, resolved). I was in the room when a man in Stuttgart built a device that briefly made gravity optional in a six-block radius (Dalton fixed it, then called his mother to tell her, then spent three hours upset because she said "That's nice, sweetheart" and he felt she was being dismissive). narrative_idea_gen_original_prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin)

Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder.

Market stalls sell handwoven fabrics dyed in pigments not found on Earth. Length: 1000 words.
